chapter.name: Lines and Angles
chapter.blurb: The building blocks of plane geometry -- points, line segments, lines, rays and angles -- how to compare angles by superimposition and other methods, the straight and right angle, measuring angles in degrees with a protractor, drawing angles of a given measure, and classifying every angle by its degree measure including reflex angles.

scope_in.item: Identify a point as a precise location with no length, breadth or height, denoted by a capital letter
Line segment as the shortest path between two points A and B (including the end points), denoted AB or BA
Line as a line segment extended endlessly in both directions, denoted AB (through two named points) or by a single small letter such as l or m; any two points determine a unique line
Ray as a portion of a line starting at one point (its starting/initial point) and extending endlessly in one direction, named with the starting point written first, e.g. AP
A ray's name is not reversible: swapping the two letters names a different ray with a different starting point

Angle as the figure formed by two rays sharing a common starting point (the vertex); the rays are the arms; naming an angle with the vertex letter in the middle, e.g. angle DBE or angle EBD, using the symbol for angle
Size of an angle as the amount of rotation or turn needed about the vertex to move one ray onto the other
Comparing two angles by superimposition: matching vertices and one pair of arms to see which angle is larger, smaller, or that they are equal
Comparing angles without superimposition using a transparent circular overlay marked with the arm positions
Comparing angles using rotating-arm models made from straws and a paper clip, and a matching angle-shaped slit; the angle depends only on the amount of turn, not on the arm lengths
Straight angle as the angle of a half turn, with its two arms lying in a straight line
Right angle as exactly half of a straight angle, obtained by folding; perpendicular lines as two lines meeting at a right angle
Classifying an angle as acute (less than a right angle) or obtuse (greater than a right angle, less than a straight angle)
The degree as the unit obtained by dividing a full turn into 360 equal parts; a full turn measures 360 degrees, a straight angle 180 degrees, a right angle 90 degrees
Reading an angle's degree measure using a circular or semicircular protractor, including choosing the correct one of its two scales
Constructing a paper protractor by repeated folding, obtaining the 90, 45, 22.5-degree (and similar) marks
Bisecting an angle by folding so the two resulting parts are equal, and identifying the angle bisector as the line/ray dividing a given angle into two equal angles
Correctly placing a protractor -- centre on the vertex, one arm aligned to the 0-degree mark -- before reading a measure, and spotting common protractor-reading errors
Drawing an angle of a given degree measure using a protractor: draw a base ray, align the protractor's centre and 0-degree line to it, mark the point at the required degree, and join with a ruler
Classifying any angle purely by its degree measure as acute (0 to 90), right (90), obtuse (90 to 180), straight (180), or reflex (180 to 360)

scope_out.item: Complementary and supplementary angles (pairs of angles summing to 90 or 180 degrees)
scope_out.reason: This chapter classifies a single angle by its own measure only; angle pairs and their sums are not introduced here

scope_out.item: Compass-and-straightedge construction of specific angles (e.g. 60 degrees) or of an angle bisector using compass arcs
scope_out.reason: This chapter's constructions use only a protractor and paper-folding; compass constructions belong to Chapter 8, Playing with Constructions

scope_out.item: The angle sum property of a triangle (that its three angles add to 180 degrees) as an established rule
scope_out.reason: The book poses this only as an open measure-and-discover activity (p. 43) and explicitly defers the explanation to 'a later year'; it is not stated as a rule in this chapter's summary

scope_out.item: Parallel lines, transversals, and the angle relationships they create (corresponding, alternate, co-interior angles)
scope_out.reason: Not introduced anywhere in this chapter

scope_out.item: Named theorems about angles at a point or on a line (e.g. linear pair, angles round a point summing to 360 degrees) stated as general rules
scope_out.reason: The book only works these out for specific figures (e.g. the 24 spokes of the Ashoka Chakra) as activities; it never names or states them as general theorems in this chapter
All degree measures in this chapter are whole or half-degree values read off a protractor; finer subdivisions are not used

concepts.name: Point, Line Segment and Line
concepts.description: The basic building blocks of geometry: a point as a location, a line segment as the shortest join of two points, and a line as a line segment extended endlessly both ways.
concepts.idea: A line segment is the shortest path between two points; stretching it forever in both directions gives a line.
concepts.rule: A point is denoted by a capital letter. The line segment joining A and B is written AB or BA. The line through A and B is written AB (or a small letter like l or m) and extends forever both ways; any two points determine exactly one line.
concepts.example: The line segment PQ has two end points P and Q; extending it endlessly in both directions gives the line PQ.

questions.q: Which of these best describes a point?
questions.a: A precise location with no length, breadth or height
o: A precise location with no length, breadth or height
A shape with length but no breadth
A path with two end points
A mark that extends endlessly in one direction

questions.q: The line segment joining points A and B can be written as
questions.a: AB or BA
o: AB with an arrow pointing from A to B only

questions.q: A ____ is obtained by extending a line segment endlessly in both directions.
questions.a: line

questions.q: Which statement about a line is NOT true?
questions.a: A line has two end points
o: A line has two end points
A line extends endlessly in both directions
A line can be named using a single small letter such as l
Two points determine a unique line

questions.q: Any two distinct points determine
questions.a: exactly one line
o: exactly one line segment only, never a line
no line unless a third point is given

questions.q: A line segment differs from a line because a line segment
questions.a: has two fixed end points, while a line extends endlessly both ways
o: has two fixed end points, while a line extends endlessly both ways
extends endlessly in one direction only
has no end points at all
can be named using only a single small letter

questions.q: The line segment from A to B, together with A and B, is the ____ route from A to B.
questions.a: shortest

questions.q: If a line is named using a single letter, it is usually written as
questions.a: a small letter such as l or m
o: a small letter such as l or m
a capital letter such as L or M

questions.q: Explain the difference between a line segment AB and a line AB, using the idea of end points.
questions.a: A line segment AB has two fixed end points A and B and is of finite length, while a line AB has no end points -- it is imagined to extend endlessly in both directions.
s: States that a line segment AB has two fixed end points and finite length
States that a line AB has no end points and extends endlessly both ways

questions.q: Kiran marks two points C and D on a page and joins them by the shortest possible path. What has Kiran drawn?
questions.a: The line segment CD

questions.q: If the line segment ST is extended endlessly on both sides, the figure obtained is called the ____ ST.
questions.a: line

questions.q: Four points, no three of which lie on one line, are marked on a page. Through how many different pairs of points can lines be drawn?

P and Q are two points on a sheet of paper. Ravi draws the line segment PQ, and then extends it beyond both P and Q without stopping. Name the figure Ravi has now drawn, and explain why it can no longer be labelled with just two end points.
questions.a: Ravi has drawn the line PQ. It cannot be labelled with two end points because a line has no end points -- it extends endlessly in both directions, unlike the line segment he started with.
s: Names the figure as the line PQ
Explains that a line has no end points as it extends endlessly both ways

questions.q: Points L, M and N lie on the same straight line, with M between L and N. Name all the line segments that can be formed using these three points, and state how many there are.
questions.a: The line segments are LM, MN and LN -- three in total.
s: Names the three line segments LM, MN and LN
States the correct count of three

questions.q: Five points are marked on a page such that no three of them lie on the same line. Deepa wants to draw a line through every possible pair of these five points. How many lines will she draw in total? Show your reasoning.
questions.a: Each pair of the 5 points gives one line. The number of pairs is (5 x 4) / 2 = 10, so Deepa will draw 10 lines.
s: Recognises that each pair of points gives exactly one line
Sets up the pair-counting calculation (5 x 4) / 2
Obtains the correct total of 10 lines

questions.q: Assertion (A): The line segment PQ has two end points, P and Q. Reason (R): Two lines meeting at a right angle are called perpendicular. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, R is true
A is true, R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

questions.q: Consider: (I) A line has a fixed length that can be measured with a ruler. (II) Any two points determine exactly one line passing through both of them. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only II

questions.q: A student claims: 'Since a line segment is part of a line, a line segment and the line containing it must have the same length.' Evaluate this claim, referring to the idea of end points and endless extension.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. A line segment AB has a fixed, measurable length between its two end points A and B, but the line containing it has no end points and extends endlessly in both directions, so it has no length that can be measured or compared to the line segment's length.
s: States that the claim is wrong
Explains that the line segment has fixed, measurable length between its end points
Explains that the line extends endlessly and so has no length to measure

questions.q: A student writes 'A line has two end points, just like a line segment.' Identify the mistake and give the correct statement.
questions.a: The mistake is thinking a line has end points. A line has no end points at all -- only a line segment has two fixed end points; a line extends endlessly in both directions.
s: Identifies that the mistake is claiming a line has end points
Gives the correct statement that a line has no end points and extends endlessly

questions.q: Describe three points on a page so that no two of them coincide and not all three lie on one line, then list every line segment formed by joining them in pairs.
questions.a: Example: mark points X, Y and Z so that no two of them coincide and not all three lie on one line. Joining them in pairs gives three distinct line segments: XY, YZ and XZ.
s: Describes three distinct, non-coincident points
Lists all three pairs correctly as line segments
Confirms the three line segments are all different

concepts.name: Ray and Angle: Naming, Vertex and Arms
concepts.description: A ray as a one-directional endless portion of a line starting at a fixed point, and an angle as the figure formed by two rays sharing a common starting point.
concepts.idea: A ray remembers where it starts; an angle is what you get when two rays share that starting point.
concepts.rule: A ray starting at O and passing through P is named OP, with the starting point always written first; OP and PO are not the same ray. An angle formed by rays BD and BE, sharing vertex B, is named angle DBE or angle EBD, with the vertex letter always in the middle.
concepts.example: Ray OA starts at O and goes on forever through A. Rays BD and BE meeting at B form angle DBE.

questions.q: A ray is a portion of a line that
questions.a: starts at one point and extends endlessly in one direction
o: starts at one point and extends endlessly in one direction
has no starting point at all

questions.q: In the name of an angle such as angle DBE, the middle letter B stands for the
questions.a: vertex of the angle

questions.q: The two rays that form an angle are called the ____ of the angle.
questions.a: arms

questions.q: A ray starting at O passes through both A and B. Which of these is NOT an acceptable name for this ray?
questions.a: BO
o: the ray from O through A and B

questions.q: An angle is formed when two rays
questions.a: share a common starting point
o: are extended from two different points that never meet

questions.q: Angle DBE and angle EBD refer to
questions.a: the same angle
o: two different angles with different vertices
two rays instead of an angle
an angle only if D and E are the same point

questions.q: In naming an angle, the letter for the ____ is always written in the middle.
questions.a: vertex

questions.q: Ray PQ and ray QP are
questions.a: different rays, because they start at different points
o: different rays, because they start at different points
the same ray, just written in reverse
the same ray only if P and Q are both marked with an arrow
different rays only when P and Q are far apart

questions.q: A ray starts at point M and passes through point N. Explain why this ray cannot correctly be called ray NM.
questions.a: A ray is named by writing its starting point first. Since this ray starts at M, it must be called ray MN. Calling it ray NM would wrongly suggest the ray starts at N instead of M.
s: States that a ray's name must begin with its starting point
Explains that NM would wrongly suggest N is the starting point

questions.q: Rays XY and XZ share the starting point X. What figure do they form?
questions.a: An angle with vertex X

questions.q: Two rays OP and OQ meeting at the common point O form the angle written as angle POQ or angle ____.
questions.a: QOP

questions.q: A ray starts at point O and passes through point A. If another point B also lies on this ray beyond A, which of these correctly names the same ray?
questions.a: OB

questions.q: Three rays OA, OB and OC all start at the same point O. Name all the different angles that can be formed by taking these rays two at a time, and state how many there are.
questions.a: The angles are angle AOB, angle BOC and angle AOC -- three in total.
s: Names the three possible angles AOB, BOC and AOC
States the correct count of three

questions.q: Ray OP starts at O and passes through P. A student says 'if I extend OP further past P, it becomes a longer ray.' Explain whether the student is correct, using the idea of endless extension.
questions.a: The student is not quite correct in saying it becomes 'longer' -- a ray already extends endlessly in one direction from O, so it has no end to extend further; drawing more of it just shows more of the same ray, not a longer one.
s: States that the ray already extends endlessly, so it has no end to extend
Explains that showing more of it is the same ray, not a new longer one

questions.q: Four rays OA, OB, OC and OD all start at the same point O, arranged so that no two of them lie on the same line. How many different angles can be named by choosing pairs of these rays? Explain the reasoning you used to count them.
questions.a: Each pair of the 4 rays forms one angle. The number of pairs is (4 x 3) / 2 = 6, so 6 different angles can be named.
s: Recognises that each pair of rays gives exactly one angle
Sets up the pair-counting calculation (4 x 3) / 2
Obtains the correct total of 6 angles

questions.q: Assertion (A): Ray OA and ray AO are the same ray. Reason (R): A ray is completely determined by its starting point and the direction in which it travels.
questions.a: A is false but R is true
o: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false

questions.q: Consider: (I) Every ray has exactly one starting point. (II) The order of the two letters used to name a ray can always be swapped without changing its meaning. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only I

questions.q: A student claims: 'Naming an angle as angle DBE or angle EBD is just like naming a ray as BD or DB -- both orders always mean the same thing.' Evaluate this claim, comparing how an angle is named to how a ray is named.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. For an angle, angle DBE and angle EBD do mean the same angle because the vertex B is fixed in the middle and only the arms are being listed in a different order. But for a ray, BD and DB are NOT the same -- a ray's name must start with its actual starting point, so swapping the order changes which point is claimed to be the starting point.
s: States that the claim is wrong
Explains that angle DBE and angle EBD are the same because the vertex stays in the middle
Explains that BD and DB are different rays because the starting point changes

questions.q: A student names the ray starting at point Q and passing through point R as 'ray RQ.' Identify the mistake and give the correct name.
questions.a: The mistake is writing the starting point second. Since the ray starts at Q, it should be named ray QR, with Q written first.
s: Identifies that the starting point was written in the wrong position
Gives the correct name, ray QR, with Q first

questions.q: Describe three rays of your own, all starting from the same point, and then name every angle formed by taking them two at a time.
questions.a: Example: rays OP, OQ and OR all start at point O. Taking them two at a time gives three angles: angle POQ, angle QOR and angle POR.
s: Describes three rays sharing one common starting point
Lists all three pairs as angles
Names each angle correctly with the shared vertex in the middle

concepts.name: Comparing Angles
concepts.description: Deciding which of two angles is larger, smaller or equal, using superimposition and other methods, and recognising that an angle's size depends only on the amount of turn between its arms.
concepts.idea: An angle's size is how much you have to turn one arm to reach the other -- so comparing angles means comparing amounts of turn, not the lengths of the arms drawn.
concepts.rule: Two angles can be compared by superimposition: place one on the other with vertices together and one pair of arms matching; if the other arms also match, the angles are equal, otherwise whichever arm falls outside is the larger angle. The size of an angle does not change if its arms are drawn longer or shorter.
concepts.example: If angle ABC is placed over angle PQR with vertex B on vertex Q and arm BA on arm QP, and arm BC falls inside angle PQR, then angle PQR is the larger angle.

questions.q: Comparing two angles by placing one exactly over the other is called
questions.a: superimposition

questions.q: When comparing angles by superimposition, which parts must be placed together first?
questions.a: The vertices of both angles
o: The end points of the arms only

questions.q: If, after superimposing two angles, both pairs of arms coincide exactly, the two angles are ____.
questions.a: equal

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a valid way to compare the sizes of two angles?
questions.a: Comparing the lengths of the arms drawn for each angle
o: Comparing the lengths of the arms drawn for each angle
Superimposing one angle on the other
Using a transparent circular overlay marked with both arms
Using a rotating-arm model and a matching slit

questions.q: The size of an angle depends on
questions.a: the amount of turn between its two arms
o: the amount of turn between its two arms
the length of the arms drawn
the colour used to draw the angle
the position of the angle on the page

questions.q: If angle AOB is superimposed on angle XOY with vertices and one arm matching, and arm OB falls exactly on arm OY, the two angles are
questions.a: equal in size
o: equal only if OA equals OX in length

questions.q: Drawing the arms of an angle longer does NOT change the angle's ____.
questions.a: size

questions.q: Two students draw the same angle, but one draws it with much longer arms. Their angles are
questions.a: equal in size, since size depends on the amount of turn, not the arm length
o: equal in size, since size depends on the amount of turn, not the arm length
different in size, since one has longer arms
impossible to compare without a protractor
equal only if both students used the same colour pen

questions.q: Explain how a transparent circular sheet can be used to compare two angles without superimposing the angles directly on top of each other.
questions.a: The circle is placed with its centre on the vertex of the first angle, and the points where its arms cross the circle's edge are marked. The same circle is then placed on the second angle in the same way, using one matching arm, to see whether the other marked point falls inside, outside, or exactly on the second angle's arm, telling us which angle is larger, smaller or equal.
s: Explains marking the points where the first angle's arms cross the circle
Explains using the same circle on the second angle to compare the arm positions

questions.q: Rohan superimposes angle ABC on angle PQR and finds that arm BC falls inside angle PQR after the vertices and arms BA, QP are matched. Which angle is larger?
questions.a: angle PQR

questions.q: A rotating-arm model made from two straws will pass through a matching slit only when its angle is ____ to the angle of the slit.
questions.a: equal

questions.q: A rotating-arm model passes through a slit, but a second rotating arm with a wider angle does not pass through the same slit. What can be concluded?
questions.a: The slit's angle equals the first rotating arm's angle, and is smaller than the second's angle
o: The slit's angle equals the first rotating arm's angle, and is smaller than the second's angle
The slit's angle is larger than both rotating arms' angles
Both rotating arms have exactly the slit's angle
The second rotating arm's angle is smaller than the slit's angle

questions.q: Meena draws angle XOY with short arms and angle PQR with much longer arms, but both angles look the same amount of 'opening'. Using superimposition, how would you check whether they are actually equal, and what result would confirm they are?
questions.a: Superimpose the two angles with their vertices together and one pair of arms matching; if the second pair of arms also matches exactly, regardless of the different arm lengths, the two angles are equal.
s: Describes superimposing the vertices and one pair of arms
States that the second pair of arms also matching confirms equal angles, regardless of arm length

questions.q: Two cranes open their beaks to form angles that cannot easily be superimposed directly. Suggest a method other than direct superimposition to find out which crane opens its beak wider, and briefly describe how it works.
questions.a: Use a transparent circular sheet: place its centre on the vertex of one crane's angle and mark where the arms cross the circle's edge, then place the same circle on the other crane's angle in the same way to see which marked arm falls further around the circle -- that crane's angle is wider.
s: Suggests using a transparent circular overlay
Describes marking and comparing the arm positions on the circle to decide which is wider

questions.q: Three rotating-arm models, X, Y and Z, are compared using a single slit cut to match model X's angle. Model X passes through the slit. Model Y does not pass through, and when compared by superimposition with X, Y's arms fall outside X's arms. Model Z does not pass through either, and its arms fall inside X's arms when superimposed. Arrange the angles of X, Y and Z from smallest to largest, explaining your reasoning.
questions.a: Z is smallest, then X, then Y is largest. Z's arms fall inside X's when superimposed, so Z's angle is smaller than X's. X passes through the slit, so X's angle equals the slit's angle. Y's arms fall outside X's, so Y's angle is larger than X's.
s: States the correct order Z, X, Y from smallest to largest
Explains that Z is smaller than X because its arms fall inside on superimposition
Explains that Y is larger than X because its arms fall outside on superimposition

questions.q: Assertion (A): When angle ABC is placed over angle PQR with vertex B on vertex Q and arm BA on arm QP, and arm BC falls inside angle PQR, then angle PQR is the larger angle. Reason (R): Two angles can only be compared by superimposition if their arms are drawn to exactly the same length. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, R is false
o: A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

questions.q: Consider: (I) Superimposing two angles requires their vertices to be placed together. (II) An angle drawn with longer arms is always bigger than one drawn with shorter arms. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only I

questions.q: A student claims: 'Since I cannot superimpose the angles made by two cranes opening their beaks in a photograph, there is no way to compare them.' Evaluate this claim, describing at least one method from the chapter that could still be used.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. Even without superimposing the actual photograph, a transparent circular sheet can be used: placing its centre on each crane's vertex in turn and marking where the arms cross the circle's edge lets us compare how far apart the marks are around the circle, telling us which angle is larger without moving the original angles on top of each other.
s: States that the claim is wrong
Describes using a transparent circular overlay as an alternative method
Explains how marking the arm positions on the circle allows comparison

questions.q: A student says 'the angle with the longer arms drawn is definitely the bigger angle.' Identify the mistake and give the correct idea.
questions.a: The mistake is judging angle size by arm length. The size of an angle depends only on the amount of turn between its arms, not on how long the arms happen to be drawn; the two angles must actually be compared, for example by superimposition.
s: Identifies the mistake of judging size by arm length
States the correct idea that size depends on the amount of turn, to be checked by comparison

questions.q: Describe two angles of your own that look very different at first glance -- one drawn with short arms and one with long arms -- but are actually equal, and explain how you would prove they are equal without measuring in degrees.
questions.a: Example: draw angle ABC with short arms and angle PQR with long arms, both opened to the same amount of turn. To prove they are equal without measuring in degrees, superimpose them by placing vertex B on vertex Q and arm BA along arm QP; if arm BC then falls exactly on arm QR, the two angles are equal.
s: Describes two angles with visibly different arm lengths
States that superimposition is the method to use
Correctly describes matching vertices and arms to confirm equality

concepts.name: Straight Angle, Right Angle, and Acute/Obtuse Angles
concepts.description: Recognising a straight angle as a half turn, a right angle as exactly half of a straight angle, perpendicular lines, and classifying angles as acute or obtuse by comparing them to a right angle.
concepts.idea: A right angle is found by folding a straight angle exactly in half; angles smaller than that fold are acute, and angles bigger than it (but less than the straight angle) are obtuse.
concepts.rule: A straight angle is formed by a half turn, with its arms lying in a straight line. Folding a straight angle exactly in half gives two equal right angles; two lines meeting at a right angle are called perpendicular. An angle less than a right angle is acute; an angle greater than a right angle but less than a straight angle is obtuse.
concepts.example: Angle AOB is a straight angle because A, O and B lie in a straight line; folding it exactly in half through O gives two right angles.

questions.q: A straight angle is formed when the two arms of an angle
questions.a: lie in a straight line

questions.q: Two lines that meet to form a right angle are called
questions.a: perpendicular lines

questions.q: An angle smaller than a right angle is called an ____ angle.
questions.a: acute

questions.q: Which of these is NOT true of a right angle?
questions.a: It is formed by a full turn
o: It is formed by a full turn
It is exactly half of a straight angle
Its arms resemble the shape of the letter L
Two lines meeting at this angle are called perpendicular

questions.q: An obtuse angle is
questions.a: greater than a right angle but less than a straight angle
o: greater than a right angle but less than a straight angle
exactly equal to a right angle

questions.q: Folding a straight angle exactly in half through its vertex produces
questions.a: two equal right angles
o: one obtuse and one acute angle

questions.q: A straight angle is formed by a ____ turn.
questions.a: half

questions.q: Ray OC divides straight angle AOB into angle AOC and angle COB. If angle AOC is acute, then angle COB must be
questions.a: obtuse

questions.q: Explain, using the idea of folding, why a right angle is described as 'exactly half of a straight angle.'
questions.a: A straight angle has its arms in a straight line; folding the paper so that one arm lands exactly on the other creates a crease that splits the straight angle into two equal parts, and each equal part is called a right angle -- so a right angle is exactly half the straight angle it was folded from.
s: Describes folding a straight angle so one arm lands on the other
Explains that this creates two equal parts, each called a right angle

questions.q: A door is opened so that it stands exactly perpendicular to the wall it is hinged to. The angle between the door and the wall is
questions.a: a right angle

questions.q: An angle that is greater than a right angle but less than a straight angle is called an ____ angle.
questions.a: obtuse

questions.q: Angle PQR is a straight angle, and ray QS is drawn so that angle PQS is obtuse. What must angle SQR be?
questions.a: acute

questions.q: A window frame has two straight edges meeting at its corner. Using a folded paper right angle as a check, you find the corner does not match the fold exactly on one side. What can you conclude about the angle at that corner, and what should it have been for the window to be perfectly rectangular?
questions.a: The corner's angle is not exactly a right angle (it is either a bit more or a bit less than 90 degrees, i.e. slightly obtuse or slightly acute); for the window to be perfectly rectangular, every corner should be exactly a right angle.
s: Concludes the corner angle is not exactly a right angle
States that a perfectly rectangular window needs right angles at every corner

questions.q: A straight angle AOB is divided by ray OC into two angles that a student says are 'definitely both right angles.' Is the student's statement always true? Explain.
questions.a: No, the student's statement is not always true. Ray OC divides the straight angle into two right angles only if OC is positioned exactly halfway between OA and OB; for any other position of OC, the two parts will be one acute and one obtuse angle instead.
s: States that the statement is not always true
Explains that only the halfway position of OC gives two right angles, otherwise one acute and one obtuse result

questions.q: A carpenter checks a table corner with a folded-paper right angle and finds the corner's angle is clearly wider than the fold, though the two edges of the table still meet in a way that looks almost like a straight line. Explain what kind of angle the corner most likely is, whether it could be mistaken for a straight angle, and how the carpenter could be sure using the fold.
questions.a: The corner's angle is most likely obtuse, since it is wider than a right angle. It could easily be mistaken for a straight angle if it is close to 180 degrees, but as long as the two edges are not lying exactly along one straight line, it remains obtuse rather than straight. concepts.name: Measuring Angles in Degrees
concepts.description: The degree as the standard unit for angle measure, reading angle sizes with a protractor, and bisecting an angle.
concepts.idea: Dividing a full turn into 360 equal parts gives a fixed-size unit, the degree, that lets us give any angle an exact number instead of just comparing it to another angle.
concepts.rule: A full turn measures 360 degrees, so a straight angle measures 180 degrees and a right angle measures 90 degrees. A protractor is used to read an angle's degree measure by placing its centre on the vertex and aligning one arm to the 0-degree mark. The line that bisects an angle divides it into two equal angles and is called the angle bisector.
concepts.example: If the arms of angle KAL span 30 of the protractor's 1-degree markings, then angle KAL measures 30 degrees.

Evaluate whether this reading is possible directly, and explain how a semicircular protractor's scale is limited compared to what the actual angle needs.
questions.a: The reading is not possible directly. A semicircular protractor's scales only run from 0 to 180 degrees, so it cannot directly show a measure like 250 degrees, which is a reflex angle greater than a straight angle. To find such a measure, the student would need to measure the remaining angle (360 minus 250 = 110 degrees) with the semicircular protractor and subtract it from 360, or use a full circular protractor instead.

concepts.name: Drawing Angles and Classifying by Measure
concepts.description: Constructing an angle of a given degree measure with a protractor, and classifying any angle -- straight, right, acute, obtuse or reflex -- purely from its degree measure.
concepts.idea: Once an angle has a degree measure, both drawing it and naming its type become a matter of reading and comparing numbers on a protractor.
concepts.rule: To draw an angle of a given measure: draw a base ray, place the protractor's centre on its starting point with the ray aligned to 0 degrees, mark a point at the required degree on the matching scale, then join the points with a ruler. By degree measure, angles are classified as acute (more than 0 and less than 90 degrees), right (exactly 90 degrees), obtuse (more than 90 and less than 180 degrees), straight (exactly 180 degrees), or reflex (more than 180 and less than 360 degrees).
concepts.example: An angle measuring 250 degrees is a reflex angle, because 250 is greater than 180 and less than 360.

questions.q: A student is asked to draw an angle of 205 degrees using a standard semicircular (180-degree) protractor. Explain why this cannot be marked directly in one step, and describe a method to draw it correctly.
questions.a: A semicircular protractor's scale only runs from 0 to 180 degrees, so 205 degrees, being a reflex angle greater than 180, cannot be marked directly on it in one step. To draw it, first find the remaining angle: 360 - 205 = 155 degrees. Draw the base ray, then use the protractor to mark a 155-degree angle on the other side of the base ray (going the opposite way around); the reflex angle on the original side will then be exactly 205 degrees.
s: Explains that a semicircular protractor only reads up to 180 degrees
Computes the supplementary-to-360 measure as 155 degrees
Describes marking the 155-degree angle on the other side to leave the correct 205-degree reflex angle
